name: Greek Pantheon
description: The Greek pantheon encompasses the gods and goddesses of ancient Greek mythology, centered on Mount Olympus and featuring the twelve Olympians who ruled after the Titanomachy.
detailedHistory:
## Origins of the Olympians

The Greek pantheon emerged from the mingling of indigenous Pelasgian beliefs with the sky-god traditions of invading Hellenic tribes.

### The Golden Age

Before the gods, there were the Titans, ruled by Cronus. This was a time of peace and prosperity, but also stagnation. The rise of Zeus and the Olympians marked the beginning of a new cosmic order—civilization, law, and justice replacing the raw elemental forces of the Titans.

### Mount Olympus

The twelve major gods (Olympians) dwelt on Mount Olympus, the highest peak in Greece. From their divine palaces, they observed human affairs, intervening to reward piety or punish hubris.

name: Norse Pantheon
description: The Norse pantheon includes the Aesir and Vanir gods of Scandinavian mythology, centered in Asgard and featuring stories of creation, heroism, and the prophesied end of the world known as Ragnarok.
detailedHistory:
## The World Tree and Ragnarok

Norse mythology centers on Yggdrasil, the Ash Tree connecting the nine worlds. The Aesir (sky gods) and Vanir (earth gods) eventually unified after a war.

### The Prophecy

Unique among mythologies, the Norse gods know their end. **Ragnarok** is the prophesied twilight of the gods, where they will battle the frost giants and chaos monsters, resulting in the destruction and renewal of the world.

name: Egyptian Pantheon
description: The Egyptian pantheon encompasses the gods and goddesses of ancient Egypt, featuring creation deities, solar worship, the afterlife, and the eternal struggle between order (Ma'at) and chaos (Isfet).
detailedHistory:
## Gods of the Nile

Egyptian mythology is one of the longest-enduring religious systems in history. It focused heavily on the afterlife, the sun's journey, and the maintenance of *Ma'at* (cosmic order).

### The Afterlife

The Egyptians believed the soul faced judgment in the Hall of Truth, where the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at. Only the righteous could enter the Field of Reeds.

name: Roman Pantheon
description: The Roman pantheon adapted Greek mythology while emphasizing duty, piety, and state religion. Romans identified their gods with Greek counterparts but maintained distinct rituals, festivals, and a practical approach to divine favor.

name: Hindu Pantheon
description: Hindu mythology encompasses thousands of years of religious and philosophical tradition from the Indian subcontinent. Centered on the Trimurti (Brahma the Creator, Vishnu the Preserver, and Shiva the Destroyer) and featuring countless gods, goddesses, and avatars.

name: Japanese Pantheon
description: Shinto (Way of the Kami) is the indigenous spirituality of Japan, featuring countless kami (divine spirits or gods) associated with natural phenomena, ancestors, and sacred places.

name: Celtic Pantheon
description: The deities of the Celtic peoples, associated with nature, magic, war, and sovereignty. Known for the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish mythology.

name: Aztec Pantheon
description: A complex pantheon centered on duality, sacrifice, and the sun, demanding blood sacrifice to sustain the cosmos.

name: Chinese Pantheon
description: A vast bureaucracy of gods, spirits, and immortals reflecting the imperial government on earth, blending Taoism, Buddhism, and folk religion.
detailedHistory:
## The Celestial Bureaucracy

Chinese mythology is unique in structuring its divine realm as a mirror of the imperial government on Earth. The Jade Emperor presides over a complex hierarchy of gods, spirits, and immortals, each with specific ranks, duties, and jurisdictions. This 'celestial bureaucracy' includes ministries of thunder, rain, fire, and pestilence, with deities promoted or demoted based on their performance.

### Three Traditions United

Chinese mythology synthesizes three major traditions: **Taoism** (with its emphasis on immortality, nature, and the Tao), **Buddhism** (introducing bodhisattvas like Guanyin and concepts of karma), and **folk religion** (featuring local gods, ancestor worship, and nature spirits). This syncretism allows figures like Sun Wukong to be simultaneously a Taoist immortal, a Buddhist disciple, and a folk hero.

### The Quest for Immortality

A central theme is the pursuit of immortality through cultivation (xiu lian). Through meditation, moral conduct, and alchemical practices, mortals can become immortals (xian) and join the celestial hierarchy. This reflects the Taoist belief that the human body can be transformed through spiritual practice.

### Heaven, Earth, and the Underworld

The cosmos is divided into three realms: Heaven (Tian), ruled by the Jade Emperor; Earth (Di), inhabited by humans and nature spirits; and the Underworld (Diyu), governed by Yan Wang (King Yama) where souls are judged and may be punished or reincarnated. The interconnection of these realms drives many myths.

name: Mesopotamian Pantheon
description: The gods of ancient Sumer, Akkad, and Babylon - humanity's oldest recorded mythology. These deities shaped the earliest written literature and influenced all subsequent Near Eastern religions.
detailedHistory:
## The Cradle of Civilization

Mesopotamian mythology represents humanity's oldest recorded religious tradition, emerging from the fertile crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. The Sumerians, who built the first cities around 3500 BCE, developed a complex pantheon that was later adopted and adapted by the Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians.

### The Great Gods

The highest triad consisted of Anu (sky), Enlil (wind/storms), and Enki (water/wisdom). Below them ruled a celestial council of great gods who determined the fates of humans and the cosmos. Unlike later monotheistic traditions, these gods were not morally perfect but displayed human emotions and conflicts.

### The Temple Economy

Mesopotamian cities were theocracies centered on the ziggurat temple, considered the literal dwelling place of the city's patron deity. The entire economy was organized around temple offerings, and kings ruled as stewards of the gods. The earliest written texts (cuneiform) were temple records, hymns, and myths.

name: African Traditions
culture: Yoruba, Akan, and other African traditions
description: A collection of distinct African religious and storytelling traditions. Yoruba orishas appear alongside Akan figures such as Anansi and Nyame, and beings from other regions. These entries do not form a single shared pantheon.
detailedHistory:
## Distinct traditions, shared collection

This collection brings together entries from several African traditions for browsing. It does not imply a common religion, origin, or historical period. Anansi and Nyame belong to Akan traditions; the Yoruba orishas have their own religious contexts.

### Yoruba traditions

Many entries in this collection concern Yoruba religion, rooted in southwestern Nigeria and neighboring Benin. Orishas connect religious practice with particular places, communities, and aspects of life. Ifa divination is one part of this living tradition.

### Akan storytelling

Anansi and Nyame appear in Akan-Ashanti tales, including the account of Anansi obtaining stories from Nyame. The version included here follows R. S. Rattray's collected account; it is one recorded version rather than a universal telling.

### Reading across traditions

Follow each entry's cultural description and references. Similar roles, such as creator or trickster, do not make figures interchangeable. The broader collection also contains beings from other African regions; their inclusion here should not be read as Yoruba or Akan attribution.

name: Polynesian Pantheon
description: The gods and spirits of Polynesian mythology span the vast Pacific Ocean, from Hawaii to New Zealand to Easter Island. Featuring powerful creator gods, the trickster demigod Maui, and deep connections to the sea, navigation, and volcanic forces.
detailedHistory:
## Voyagers of the Pacific

Polynesian mythology developed among the greatest ocean navigators in human history. Beginning around 1500 BCE, Polynesian peoples spread across the Pacific, carrying their gods, stories, and rituals to islands separated by thousands of miles of open ocean.

### The Polynesian Triangle

The Polynesian Triangle stretches from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand (Aotearoa) in the southwest and Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the southeast. Despite this vast expanse, the mythologies share common roots: the primordial parents Rangi (Sky Father) and Papa (Earth Mother), the great gods Tangaroa, Tane, Tu, and Rongo, and the beloved trickster demigod Maui.

### Regional Variations

While sharing common ancestors, each island group developed distinct traditions. Hawaiian mythology features the volcano goddess Pele and her rivalry with the snow goddess Poliahu. Maori tradition preserves elaborate genealogies (whakapapa) connecting humans to the gods. Samoan and Tongan traditions emphasize Tagaloa as the supreme creator.

### Oral Tradition

Polynesian mythology was preserved through oral tradition, chants (mele in Hawaiian, waiata in Maori), and ritual performances. Navigational knowledge, genealogies, and sacred stories were memorized by specialists and passed down through generations, only being written down after European contact.

name: Mesoamerican Pantheon
culture: Aztec, Maya, and related Mesoamerican traditions
description: Mesoamerican mythology encompasses Aztec, Maya, Olmec, and other pre-Columbian traditions. Featuring feathered serpent deities, cosmic cycles of creation and destruction, underworld journeys, and the belief that sacrifice sustains the universe.
detailedHistory:
## Two Thousand Years of Civilization

Mesoamerican mythology represents one of humanity's most complex and interconnected religious traditions, developing independently in the Americas over millennia. From the Olmec 'mother culture' (1500-400 BCE) through the Maya Classic period (250-900 CE) to the Aztec Empire (1300-1521 CE), these civilizations shared fundamental concepts while developing unique expressions.

### The Feathered Serpent

The figure of the feathered serpent appears throughout Mesoamerican history: as Quetzalcoatl among the Aztecs and Kukulkan among the Maya. This deity represents the union of earth (serpent) and sky (quetzal bird), embodying wind, wisdom, and the morning star. Worship of feathered serpent deities dates back to at least the Olmec era.

### Cycles of Creation and Destruction

Both Aztec and Maya traditions describe multiple world ages or 'suns' that were created and destroyed. The current world exists in a precarious balance, sustained by proper ritual observance. Time itself was cyclical, with elaborate calendars tracking sacred and agricultural cycles.

### The Underworld Journey

The Aztec Mictlan and Maya Xibalba represent perilous underworld realms that souls must traverse after death. The Maya Popol Vuh recounts the Hero Twins' journey to Xibalba, while Aztec mythology describes Quetzalcoatl's descent to Mictlan to retrieve ancestral bones.

### Sacrifice and Cosmic Debt

Mesoamerican religions understood humanity as owing a fundamental debt to the gods who sacrificed themselves to create the current world. This debt could only be repaid through offerings, including blood sacrifice, which was seen as nourishing the cosmos itself.

name: Slavic Pantheon
culture: Slavic (East, West, and Baltic-coast Slavic peoples)
description: The gods of the pre-Christian Slavic peoples, known almost entirely through hostile outside witnesses, a handful of chronicle entries, and the outlines that survived Christianization inside later folklore.
detailedHistory:
## A religion without its own scripture

No native Slavic pagan text survives. Everything known comes from outsiders (a Byzantine soldier-historian, German and Danish churchmen), from a handful of lines in Christian chronicles written after the fact, and from linguistic and archaeological reconstruction. The earliest witness is Procopius, who in his *History of the Wars* (7.14, written in the 550s CE) describes the early Slavs worshipping a single, unnamed god who "master of all" hurls the lightning, and sacrificing cattle and other victims to him, alongside rivers, nymphs, and other spirits that receive lesser offerings. He names no gods.

## East Slavic Rus': the Primary Chronicle

The *Russian Primary Chronicle* (*Povest' vremennykh let*), compiled in Kiev in the early 12th century and preserved in the Laurentian codex (1377) and Hypatian codex (c. 1425), records the treaties of 907, 945, and 971, in which the Rus' swear by their weapons, by Perun, and by Volos (Veles), "the cattle god." Under the year 980 it reports that Prince Vladimir of Kiev set up six idols on a hill outside his palace — Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh — which he had torn down and thrown into the Dnieper after his own conversion in 988. A separate strand, a gloss inserted into the Hypatian Chronicle's translation of John Malalas under 1114, borrows the frame of Greek mythology to equate Svarog with Hephaestus and to call Dazhbog "son of Svarog" — most historians read this as a learned monk's literary aside, not as direct testimony to living cult.

## West Slavic and Baltic-coast Slavs: temples the Rus' never had

Unlike the Rus', the Polabian and Pomeranian Slavs (the Redarii, the Rani of Rügen, the Pomeranians around Szczecin) built actual temple buildings with carved cult images, and German and Danish churchmen described what they saw before tearing it down: Thietmar of Merseburg (*Chronicon*, completed by 1018) on Svarozhich at the shrine of Riedegost; Adam of Bremen (*Gesta Hammaburgensis Ecclesiae Pontificum*, c. 1075), who gives a different name, Redigast, for what may be the same site; Helmold of Bosau (*Chronica Slavorum*, c. 1168) on Chernobog and on Prove and Svantevit among the Wagrians and Rani; Saxo Grammaticus (*Gesta Danorum*, Book 14, c. 1200–1216) on the four-headed idol and the white divination-horse at Arkona, destroyed by the Danish king Valdemar I in 1168; and the *Lives of Otto of Bamberg* by Ebbo and Herbord (1150s) on Triglav at Szczecin, destroyed during Otto's mission of 1124–1128.

## Reading these sources honestly

Every one of these accounts was written by a Christian outsider recording either conquest or conversion, so hostile framing and outright misunderstanding are built into the record. Vladimir's 980 pantheon was a political act by a reigning prince, not a description of a stable state religion observed from inside. Khors and Simargl are barely understood at all — their names are probably borrowed, and assigning either a confident "domain" goes beyond what the sources support. And the storm-combat between Perun and Veles, often retold on the internet as if it were an attested myth, is a 20th-century linguistic reconstruction by Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov, built by comparing later folklore, place names, and Baltic and Vedic parallels — not a story any medieval writer set down.

## What this site will not repeat

The *Book of Veles* (*Velesova kniga*), first published in the 1950s and claiming to be an ancient birch-bark chronicle, is a demonstrated 20th-century forgery: its language mixes Slavic forms from different centuries and no physical tablet has ever been produced for inspection. The Prav-Yav-Nav triad and the "god" Chislobog that circulate in popular and Rodnovery (Slavic neopagan) writing come from that forgery or from modern invention, not from any medieval source, and are not treated here as ancient. Figures such as Lada and a personified Kupala are attested only in early-modern and modern folklore, never in a pagan-era source, and are marked as such wherever they appear.

## Folk survival

After Christianization (the Rus' in 988; the Baltic Slavs by the 12th–13th century), older beliefs did not vanish but layered under a Christian surface, a pattern Russian scholarship calls *dvoeverie* ("double-faith"): Perun's thunder role was partly absorbed into the prophet Elijah, Veles's patronage of cattle partly into Saint Blaise, and a rich lower mythology of household, forest, and water spirits (domovoi, leshy, vodyanoy, rusalka) survived into the 19th-century folklore collected by ethnographers such as Alexander Afanasyev — a genuinely rich record, but of 19th-century peasant belief, not of ancient pagan theology.

name: Haudenosaunee Tradition
culture: Haudenosaunee (Six Nations / Iroquois Confederacy: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, Tuscarora)
region: Northeastern Woodlands (present-day New York State and southern Ontario)
description: A living tradition of the sovereign Haudenosaunee nations: Sky Woman's fall to Turtle Island, the twins Sapling and Flint, and the Peacemaker's founding of the Great Law of Peace, told today by the people who tell it.
detailedHistory:
## Two nations, one entry

The Haudenosaunee (People of the Longhouse, also called the Six Nations or, by an exonym, the Iroquois Confederacy) are Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and, since the early 18th century, Tuscarora nations. They are sovereign nations today, with their own governments, and Haudenosaunee people practice, teach, and retell these traditions now, not only in a documented past. This entry follows only what the Confederacy and its constituent nations share publicly themselves, plus scholarship recorded with, or in direct collaboration with, Haudenosaunee tellers, and it leaves out anything described as belonging to a specific medicine society or ceremony.

## Sky Woman, the Twins, and Turtle Island

In Haudenosaunee tradition, in the Sky World above, a woman falls through a hole torn open when a great tree is uprooted. Waterfowl slow her fall and set her on the back of a Great Turtle, who offers to bear the earth; other animals dive into the primordial waters beneath the Turtle to bring up a pawful of mud, which grows across the Turtle's back into the world, later called Turtle Island. Sky Woman's daughter is born on this new earth, and the daughter in turn gives birth to twin grandsons: the good-minded Sapling, also called Skyholder or, among the Mohawk, Teharonhiawagon ("He Holds Up the Sky"), and the hard-minded Flint (Tawiskaron), born in a way that costs their mother's life. Sapling and Flint go on to shape the features of the world, one making it fertile and easy to live in, the other making it difficult, and different nations and tellers place different weight on how their contest ends. This is cosmological tradition, not a dated history; it is told in the present tense by the people who tell it, not assigned a calendar year.

Sources for this material disagree on details large and small: which animal succeeds at diving for the mud (muskrat, in many Seneca and Onondaga tellings), what becomes of the twins' mother, and how firmly Flint is defeated versus simply withdrawn. Arthur C. Parker's *Seneca Myths and Folk Tales* (1923) and J.N.B. Hewitt's *Iroquoian Cosmology* (Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43) record these variations from Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellers by name; Hewitt was himself Tuscarora. This entry follows their lead in presenting variants side by side rather than flattening them into one version.

## The Peacemaker and the Great Law of Peace

A separate, later strand of tradition, one the Confederacy calls history as much as sacred narrative, tells how the Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa) brought the warring nations together under a shared government. In the accounts the Onondaga Nation and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy publish on their own websites, the Peacemaker, sent to end the fighting, is joined by Hiawatha (Aiionwatha), an Onondaga man who had lost his family to violence; together they persuade the powerful and feared Onondaga leader Tadodaho, described in both accounts as having snakes in his hair and a twisted body, to accept peace and become the confederacy's Firekeeper. At Onondaga Lake the nations plant the Great Tree of Peace, its roots reaching to the four directions and an eagle set at its top to watch for danger, and the Peacemaker teaches the law of "One Dish, One Spoon" and government by consensus among fifty chiefs.

Historians and the nations themselves date this founding differently: some scholars, working from an oral reference to a solar eclipse, argue for a date around 1142 CE, while archaeological approaches favor a later date, often the 15th century; the Haudenosaunee Confederacy's own materials describe it simply as "over a thousand years ago." This site does not pick a single date and presents it as it is presented by the nations: a founding whose exact year is debated, not a settled fact.

## What this entry leaves out

Material describing ceremonies of the medicine societies, the False Face Society, and other content the Haudenosaunee themselves mark as restricted or clan-specific is not included here, in line with the guidance of the sources this entry draws on. Nothing here claims to be the single correct version of any story; where tellers differ, that difference is the point.

name: Tlingit and Haida Tradition
culture: Tlingit and Haida (Northwest Coast peoples of present-day Southeast Alaska and Haida Gwaii, British Columbia)
description: A living Northwest Coast tradition of the Tlingit and Haida nations, centered on Raven: stealing daylight from a wealthy old man's boxes, and freeing the first people from a clamshell on the beach at Haida Gwaii.
detailedHistory:
## Two nations, one entry, carefully framed

Tlingit and Haida are distinct nations of the Northwest Coast, the Tlingit centered in what is now Southeast Alaska and the Haida on Haida Gwaii (formerly the Queen Charlotte Islands) in British Columbia and in southern Alaska. Both are living, sovereign peoples, and Raven's stories are told by their own tellers today, not only recorded in old books. Archaeological evidence, karst-cave finds on Haida Gwaii and remains from On Your Knees Cave in Southeast Alaska, documents human presence on this coast for at least 10,000 to 13,000 years; that figure describes how long people have lived here, not the age of any single story, since these are living oral traditions passed down and retold, not artifacts with a fixed date of composition.

## Clan property and what this site includes

Among the Tlingit especially, many stories, crests, and songs are at.óow: property owned by a specific clan, whose telling in full ceremonial context requires that clan's standing and permission. What follows here are Raven-cycle stories in the form they have been published for a general public audience, by the tellers' own nations or with their direct involvement (Sealaska Heritage Institute, the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian nations' own cultural institution, publishes Raven stories for exactly this kind of public telling) or recorded by name from specific tellers by early ethnographers. Nothing describing a restricted ceremony or a clan's exclusive at.óow is included.

## Raven

Raven, Yéil in Tlingit and, in Haida, Xuuya or Yáahl depending on dialect (Skidegate and Masset), is the central figure of this cycle: not a simple trickster but, as the poet and translator Robert Bringhurst put it of the Haida telling, one who "never actually creates anything; he made the world by stealing, exchanging, redistributing, and generally moving things around." Raven steals daylight from an old man's nested boxes at the head of the Nass River in the best-known Tlingit telling, and in a Haida telling recorded by John R. Swanton and reinterpreted in Bill Reid's sculpture *The Raven and the First Men* (1978 to 1980, Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia), he coaxes the first people out of a clamshell on the beach at Rose Spit on Haida Gwaii.

## Sources used here, and how they differ

John R. Swanton's *Tlingit Myths and Texts* (1909) and *Haida Texts and Myths* (1905) are outsider recordings, made by a non-Native ethnographer, but they record specific named Tlingit and Haida tellers and remain the fullest early written source for many of these stories. Nora Marks Dauenhauer and Richard Dauenhauer's *Haa Shuká, Our Ancestors: Tlingit Oral Narratives* (1987), edited with extensive Tlingit-language and cultural annotation, and Robert Bringhurst's translations of the Haida poets Skaay and Ghandl in *A Story as Sharp as a Knife* (1999) represent later, more collaborative scholarship, though Bringhurst's own standing to translate Haida oral literature has itself been debated within Haida and academic communities, and this site notes that debate rather than treating his translations as beyond question. Tellings differ across nation, dialect, and individual teller on details as basic as Raven's kin and exact route to the light; this entry does not force them into a single version.

name: Inca and Andean Tradition
culture: Inca (Tawantinsuyu) and the wider Quechua- and Aymara-speaking Andean world
description: The religion of the Inca state and the older Andean shrines it absorbed: Viracocha the maker rising from Lake Titicaca, Inti the Sun as ancestor of the Inca kings, and the mountain and coastal huacas of the Huarochirí Manuscript, all known through writers of the colonial era.
detailedHistory:
## Known only through the colonial filter

The Incas kept records on knotted cords (khipu) read by trained specialists, but they left no written narratives of their gods. Every story on this site was written down after the Spanish invasion of 1532, by people with their own purposes. Juan de Betanzos (1551) wrote in Cusco with the help of his wife's royal Inca kin. Cristóbal de Molina (c. 1575) questioned elders who had served in the state cult. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa (1572) interviewed Inca lineage heads for a viceroy who wanted the Incas shown as tyrants. The Inca Garcilaso de la Vega (1609), son of a Spanish captain and an Inca noblewoman, wrote from Spain decades later and presented Inca religion as a noble monotheism that anticipated Christianity. Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala (c. 1615), an Andean noble, drew and wrote a long protest to the Spanish king. And much of what survives about local gods comes from the campaigns to destroy them: the Quechua Huarochirí Manuscript (c. 1598-1608) was compiled in the circle of the extirpator Francisco de Ávila. Each of these sources is used here for what it can show, with its point of view stated.

## Two layers: the state cult and the huacas

At the top of the Inca state cult stood the Creator (called Viracocha, Con Tici Viracocha, or Pachayachachic), the Sun (Inti), the Thunder (Illapa), and the Moon (Mama Killa), whose images and chambers were housed in the Coricancha, the gold-sheathed temple at the center of Cusco. Beneath and alongside them were countless huacas: mountains, springs, stones, ancestral mummies, and regional gods with their own priests, oracles, and stories, such as Pachacamac on the coast and Pariacaca in the highlands of Huarochirí. The Inca state generally absorbed these rather than abolishing them, adding a Temple of the Sun beside Pachacamac's ancient shrine, for example, and keeping the images of conquered peoples' huacas in Cusco. Around Cusco itself, the Jesuit Bernabé Cobo later listed more than three hundred shrines arranged along imaginary lines (ceques) radiating from the Coricancha.

## Origins, ancestors, and the Sun

The Inca kings claimed descent from the Sun through the founding ancestor Manco Cápac. Chroniclers preserve two main versions of that origin: in one, told by Garcilaso, the Sun sends his son and daughter to Lake Titicaca to civilize humanity; in the other, told by Betanzos and Sarmiento, four brothers and four sisters emerge from a cave at Pacaritambo and travel to the valley of Cusco. Andean peoples more generally traced each lineage to a pacarina, a place of emergence such as a lake, spring, or cave.

## After 1572, and today

The Inca state ended with the fall of Vilcabamba and the execution of Túpac Amaru in 1572, when the Sun image called the Punchao was also captured. Andean religion did not end with it. Quechua and Aymara communities continue to make offerings to Pachamama and to the mountain lords (apus), often alongside Catholic practice, and the Inti Raymi solstice pageant has been re-staged at Sacsayhuamán in Cusco since 1944 as a civic festival reconstructed largely from Garcilaso's description.
